newsitem.title: USA: Repairs planned to fix power on stricken Mir.
newsitem.headline: Repairs planned to fix power on stricken Mir.

text.p: Repair gear for a daring rewiring job could be launched to the stricken Mir space station as early as July 5, NASA officials said on Friday.

The Russian space authorities were leaning toward an internal repair to restore electrical power lost when an out-of-control cargo ship ploughed into Mir's Spektr science module, said Frank Culbertson, who oversees NASA's missions to Mir.

Wearing bulky space suits, Mir commander Vasily Tsibliev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin would install a modified hatch in the doorway of Spektr so cables could be connected to tap electricity from the module's solar arrays. The work would be attempted in mid-July.
"This will be rehearsed very well on orbit and on the ground prior to doing it," Culbertson said.
There were no immediate plans to fix the breached hull of the damaged module.

The repair gear would be delivered to Mir aboard a new Progress cargo craft, scheduled to blast off July 5-8 from the Russian cosmodrome in the former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan. If all went according to plan, the Progress would arrive at Mir two days later.
Wednesday's orbital collision left the orbital outpost with only half its usual supply of power and robbed it of its most efficient batteries, used when the station is in darkness.
NASA's Michael Foale would sit out the repair sealed up inside the space station's Soyuz lifeboat in case the work went wrong.
If the hatch to the ruptured Spektr module could not be resealed the crew would have to abandon ship.

NASA officials asked Foale to draw up a list of science equipment and other items that could be salvaged from the damaged compartment, but he thought it would be difficult for the cosmonauts in their space suits to move inside the cluttered module.

"I'll come up with a list, although the idea of them going much further than just the entry way of Spektr seems incredible," the British-born astronaut told NASA officials at the Russian mission control.
The space station's positional pointing system failed overnight, probably because of a power glitch, but was quickly restored, Culbertson said.
All but essential equipment, including lighting, has been switched off since the accident. Life support systems were being turned on as needed.
Foale asked for extra flashlight bulbs and a hundred AA batteries to be sent up on the Progress. "We're working in the dark so much," he explained.
Additional systems were being activated as Mir's batteries charged, including the station's toilet.
"As Mike said, that was a great relief," Culbertson said.
